questions.question: Explain how subsidence and convergence act as the switch behind Africa's wet and dry climate belts, and describe the seasonal migration of the ITCZ with its consequences for rainfall calendars.
questions.expected_answer: Convergence means surface winds flowing together, usually into a low-pressure trough, forcing air upward; the rising air expands, cools adiabatically, condenses its vapour and produces convectional cloud and rain. Subsidence means air sinking from aloft and diverging at the surface; the sinking air is compressed and warms, its relative humidity falls, cloud evaporates and a temperature inversion caps the surface air, so rain is almost impossible. Equatorial Africa sits under permanent convergence and is wet all year, while the latitudes near 30 degrees north and south sit under permanent subsidence and carry the Sahara, Kalahari and Namib deserts. The ITCZ, the trough where the south-east and north-east trade winds converge, migrates with the overhead sun, lagging about a month behind it: in January it lies across southern Africa, over Angola, Zambia and Zimbabwe, driving the southern summer rains; in July it lies over the Sahel at about 15 to 20 degrees north. Places near the equator are crossed twice a year and record a double rainfall maximum; places nearer the tropics are reached once and record a single summer maximum, and a season when the belt stalls short of them brings drought.

questions.question: Describe how the Kalahari High and the two ocean current systems shape South Africa's climate, contrasting the winter and summer interior and the east and west coasts.
questions.expected_answer: The Kalahari High is the continental branch of the subtropical high-pressure belt, one of three semi-permanent anticyclones affecting the country alongside the South Atlantic and South Indian Highs. In winter it strengthens over the plateau and its subsidence inversion sinks below the level of the escarpment, so moist ocean air cannot climb onto the plateau and the Highveld winter is clear, dry and cold. In summer intense surface heating weakens the high and lifts the inversion above the escarpment, so moist Indian Ocean air floods onto the plateau and feeds the afternoon thunderstorms of Gauteng, Mpumalanga and the Free State. On the coasts, the cold Benguela Current, fed by upwelling along the west coast, chills the air from below, leaving it stable and nearly moistureless — it produces coastal fog but almost no rain, which is why the west coast is arid. The warm Mozambique-Agulhas system along the east coast heats and moistens the air from below, making it unstable and rain-ready, which is why Durban, at nearly the same latitude as Port Nolloth, is humid, green and subtropical.

questions.question: Describe how a South African synoptic weather chart is read, including pressure cells, fronts and the station model, and state the basic influence of El Niño and La Niña on southern African rainfall.
questions.expected_answer: The chart is read in a fixed order. First the isobars, drawn at four-hectopascal intervals: closed cells labelled H are anticyclones with subsiding air and clear settled weather, cells labelled L are lows with rising air and rain, and tightly packed isobars mean strong wind. The three semi-permanent highs — South Atlantic, South Indian and Kalahari — are located, and any cold front is identified as a line of triangles pointing in the direction of movement, usually approaching the Cape from the south-west with rain, a wind shift and a temperature drop behind it. Each station model is then decoded: air temperature at upper left, dew point at lower left, cloud cover in the shaded circle, and wind read from a shaft with feathers flying from the direction the wind comes from, each full feather worth ten knots. Satellite images extend the chart, showing the ITCZ as a band of thunderstorm cloud, fronts as curved cloud bars and subsidence as clear areas, while a GIS layers rainfall, dam levels and vegetation data to track drought. As basic, non-examinable knowledge: in an El Niño year the eastern Pacific warms and southern Africa usually receives below-average summer rain, as in the 2015-16 drought; in a La Niña year the Pacific cools and our summers are usually wetter, as in 2021 and 2022.
